niche.title: 8 Cranial Bones Mnemonic: Old People From Texas Eat Spiders | Skull Anatomy #shorts
niche.description:
Can you name all 8 cranial bones? One silly sentence does it: Old People From Texas Eat Spiders 🦴

O → Occipital: the back of your skull (the spinal cord exits through its foramen magnum)
P → Parietal: top and sides (a pair)
F → Frontal: your forehead
T → Temporal: right above your ears (a pair)
E → Ethmoid: tucked between your eye sockets
S → Sphenoid: the "keystone" that joins almost every other skull bone
6 names, but parietal and temporal come in pairs = 8 cranial bones.

Quick test: your spinal cord leaves the skull through which bone? Answer in the video.

niche.title: How a Cut Heals 😮
niche.description:
When you cut yourself, tiny blood vessels in your skin break open. Platelets plug the broken ends, fibrin threads trap red cells into a clot, and the clot's top dries into a scab. White blood cells squeeze out of nearby vessels to eat germs that got in. New tissue fills the gap from below, skin cells slide in under the scab, and when the scab falls off, the new tissue stays as a scar.

This is an animation, not microscopy: the cells are drawn far bigger than life, days and weeks are sped up into seconds, and in a real wound these steps overlap. Many scars fade over months.

Sources: MedlinePlu

niche.title: Why Doesn't Food Go Down Your Windpipe? 🫁
niche.description:
Air and food share one passage in your throat, and the windpipe sits right in front of the food pipe, open while you breathe. So why doesn't food fall in? Every time you swallow, your voice box lifts up and forward, a flap called the epiglottis folds back over the windpipe entrance, and your vocal folds close. Breathing stops for a moment. The top of the food pipe opens, and the food slides over the flap into it. The airway is shut for under a second, then it opens again. If something slips in anyway, you cough it back out by reflex.

niche.title: Same exercise, one small change, very different calf growth #Shorts
niche.description:
Same exercise, one small change, very different calf growth.

14 beginners trained one leg standing and the other seated for 12 weeks. The gastrocnemius grew 9 to 12 percent on the standing leg and under 2 on the seated leg. The soleus grew about the same either way.

The likely reason is the knee. The gastrocnemius crosses it, the soleus doesn't, so bending the knee leaves the gastrocnemius short and slack.

It's one small study with no control group, so treat it as a good reason to keep both variations. Do you do your calf raises standing, seated, or not at all?

Source: Kinoshita et al. 202

When you cut yourself, tiny blood vessels in your skin break open. Platelets plug the broken ends, fibrin threads trap red cells into a clot, and the clot's top dries into a scab. White blood cells squeeze out of nearby vessels to eat germs that got in. New tissue fills the gap from below, skin cells slide in under the scab, and when the scab falls off, the new tissue stays as a scar.

This is an animation, not microscopy: the cells are drawn far bigger than life, days and weeks are sped up into seconds, and in a real wound these steps overlap. Many scars fade over months.

Sources: MedlinePlu
